claim: According to the human neuropsychological literature and primate studies, the primary function of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) is the encoding and retrieval of episodic memories.
source: According to the human neuropsychological literature and primate studies, the primary function of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) is the encoding and retrieval of episodic memories (Corkin, 1984; Squire and Zola-Morgan, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corkin, 1984 and Squire and Zola-Morgan, 1991.

claim: When studying rodent behavior, the MTL is often associated with spatial navigation.
source: However, when studying rodent behavior, the MTL is often associated with spatial navigation (Moser et al., 2008; O'Keefe, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moser et al., 2008 and O'Keefe, 1976.

claim: There are some studies reporting spatial navigation cells in human MTL.
source: There are some studies reporting spatial navigation cells in human MTL (Doeller et al., 2010; e.g. Jacobs et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Doeller et al., 2010 and Jacobs et al., 2013.

claim: There are some studies reporting non-spatial cell types in rodent MTL.
source: and some studies reporting non-spatial cell types in rodent MTL (e.g. Aronov et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aronov et al., 2017.

claim: Spatial location is a powerful episodic retrieval cue.
source: Supporting this view, there is ample evidence that spatial location is a powerful episodic retrieval cue (Godden and Baddeley, 1975; Roediger, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Godden and Baddeley, 1975 and Roediger, 1980.

claim: The proposal that hippocampus represents the multimodal conjunctions that define an episode is not new.
source: The proposal that hippocampus represents the multimodal conjunctions that define an episode is not new (Marr et al., 1991; Sutherland and Rudy, 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marr et al., 1991 and Sutherland and Rudy, 1989.

claim: The proposal that hippocampal memory supports spatial/navigation ability is not new.
source: and neither is the proposal that hippocampal memory supports spatial/navigation ability (Eichenbaum, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eichenbaum, 2017.

claim: Hippocampal cells respond to the conjunction of a non-spatial attribute affixed to a specific location in 'feature in place' results.
source: This view of the hippocampus is consistent with 'feature in place' results (O'Keefe and Krupic, 2021) in which hippocampal cells respond to the conjunction of a non-spatial attribute affixed to a specific location, rather than responding more generically to any instance of a non-spatial attribute.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Krupic, 2021.

claim: The hippocampal system is not dedicated to spatial cognition and navigation, but organizes experiences in memory.
source: In reviewing the hippocampal literature, (Eichenbaum, 2017) concludes that 'the hippocampal system is not dedicated to spatial cognition and navigation, but organizes experiences in memory, for which spatial mapping and navigation are both a metaphor for and a prominent application of relational memory organization'.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eichenbaum, 2017.

claim: Most cells in MTL appear to have receptive fields related to some aspect of spatial navigation.
source: However, this memory conjunction view of the MTL must be reconciled with the rodent electrophysiology finding that most cells in MTL appear to have receptive fields related to some aspect of spatial navigation (Boccara et al., 2010; Diehl et al., 2017; Grieves and Jeffery, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boccara et al., 2010, Diehl et al., 2017, and Grieves and Jeffery, 2017.

claim: Place cells were discovered by O'Keefe in 1976.
source: if the majority of the cells in the rodent hippocampus and medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) are place cells (O'Keefe, 1976)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to O'Keefe, 1976.

claim: Grid cells were discovered by Hafting et al. in 2005.
source: grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Head direction cells were discovered by Taube et al. in 1990.
source: head direction cells (Taube et al., 1990)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Taube et al., 1990.

claim: Conjunctive grid cells that are also sensitive to head direction were discovered by Sargolini et al. in 2006.
source: conjunctive grid cells that are also sensitive to head direction (Sargolini et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: Border/boundary cells were discovered by Lever et al. in 2009 and Solstad et al. in 2008.
source: border/boundary cells (Lever et al., 2009; Solstad et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lever et al., 2009 and Solstad et al., 2008.

claim: Object-vector cells were discovered by Høydal et al. in 2019.
source: and object-vector cells (Høydal et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Høydal et al., 2019.

claim: LEC is involved in non-spatial processing.
source: Although it is generally true that LEC is involved in non-spatial processing, there is evidence that LEC provides some forms of spatial information (Knierim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knierim et al., 2014.

claim: LEC provides some forms of spatial information.
source: Although it is generally true that LEC is involved in non-spatial processing, there is evidence that LEC provides some forms of spatial information (Knierim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knierim et al., 2014.

claim: The kind of non-spatial information provided by LEC appears to be in relation to objects.
source: The kind of non-spatial information provided by LEC appears to be in relation to objects (Connor and Knierim, 2017; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Connor and Knierim, 2017 and Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: Some grid cells were found to be sound-frequency cells.
source: future studies are needed to determine the bottom-up non-spatial receptive fields that specify the non-spatial attributes K (e.g. see Aronov et al., 2017 for an example in which some grid cells were also found to be sound-frequency cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aronov et al., 2017.

claim: In the proposed memory model, place cells represent memories that are conjunctions of both spatial and non-spatial attributes.
source: In the proposed memory model, place cells represent memories that are conjunctions of both spatial and non-spatial attributes, and grid cells primarily represent the non-spatial attributes (e.g. sounds, surface texture, etc.) found throughout the two-dimensional recording enclosure.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the model.

claim: In the proposed memory model, grid cells primarily represent non-spatial attributes found throughout the two-dimensional recording enclosure.
source: In the proposed memory model, place cells represent memories that are conjunctions of both spatial and non-spatial attributes, and grid cells primarily represent the non-spatial attributes (e.g. sounds, surface texture, etc.) found throughout the two-dimensional recording enclosure.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the model.

claim: Grid cells exhibit their spatial firing pattern owing to feedback from hippocampal place cells.
source: Grid cells exhibit their spatial firing pattern owing to feedback from hippocampal place cells (i.e. a hexagonal pattern of remembered locations for the non-spatial attribute represented by a grid cell).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the model mechanism.

claim: A precise hexagonal grid is the exception rather than the rule, emerging when the animal explores a large surface that is devoid of landmarks and objects.
source: On this account, place and grid cells are best understood as the natural consequence of memory encoding and retrieval; a precise hexagonal grid is the exception rather than the rule, emerging when the animal explores a large surface that is devoid of landmarks and objects.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing when hexagonal grids emerge.

claim: The model assumes that bottom-up receptive fields of grid cells in medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) are non-spatial attributes found throughout the two-dimensional surface.
source: Figure 1 shows the core hypothesis of this proposal, which assumes that the bottom-up receptive fields of grid cells in medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) are non-spatial attributes found throughout the two-dimensional surface.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the core hypothesis of the model.

claim: Memory encoding is more likely to occur in novel situations.
source: Memory encoding is more likely to occur in novel situations (Tulving et al., 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tulving et al., 1996.

claim: Memory retrieval occurs in familiar situations.
source: whereas retrieval occurs in familiar situations (Howard et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Howard et al., 2005.

claim: The model uses border cells as the primary spatial input to hippocampus that determines place coding.
source: The model is a bidirectional two-layer network (Figure 2) in which border cells (Lever et al., 2009; Solstad et al., 2008) – a.k.a., boundary cells – are the primary spatial input to hippocampus that determines place coding.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the model architecture with citations to border cell literature.

claim: When a new memory is formed, a hippocampal place cell is recruited and the weights connecting the place cell to the entorhinal inputs are set equal to the current input values.
source: When a new memory is formed, a hippocampal place cell (or more plausibly a population of cells) is recruited and the weights connecting the place cell to the entorhinal inputs are set equal to the current input values (Grossberg and Grossberg, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Grossberg and Grossberg, 1982.

claim: The hippocampal indexing theory proposes that hippocampus indexes episodic memories.
source: This assumption is in keeping with the 'hippocampal indexing theory' of episodic memory (Teyler and Rudy, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Teyler and Rudy, 2007.

claim: The model's assumptions regarding border cells are based on the boundary vector cell (BVC) model.
source: These assumptions regarding border cells are based on the boundary vector cell (BVC) model of Barry et al., 2006.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barry et al., 2006.

claim: Rotation of a circular enclosure causes border cell representations to rotate with the enclosure but stay fixed relative to the experimental room.
source: As such, the model can explain the finding that border cell representations rotate with rotation of the enclosure (but stay fixed relative to the experimental room) in the case of a circular enclosure that lacks any salient characteristics (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Border cell representations do not rotate for a square environment, unless the rotation is 90, 180, or 270 degrees.
source: At the same time, the model can explain the finding that border cell representations do not rotate for a square environment, unless the rotation is 90, 180, or 270 degrees such that a different straight wall aligns with a salient aspect of the exterior (Krupic et al., 2015; Savelli et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Krupic et al., 2015 and Savelli et al., 2017.

claim: Human observers have difficulty re-orienting themselves in a room depending on the degree of rotational symmetry of the room.
source: Although all dimensions were assumed to be circular for reasons of mathematical convenience and parsimony, circular dimensions may relate to the finding that human observers have difficultly re-orienting themselves in a room depending on the degree of rotational symmetry of the room (Kelly et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2008.

claim: The population of grid cells lies on a torus.
source: In addition, similar to other models (Guanella et al., 2007; McNaughton et al., 2006), this simplifying assumption allows the model to capture the finding that the population of grid cells lies on a torus (Gardner et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2022.

claim: Animals can plan novel straight line paths to reach a known position.
source: Animals can plan novel straight line paths to reach a known position and evidence suggests they do so by learning Euclidean representations of space (Cheng and Gallistel, 2014; Normand and Boesch, 2009; Wilkie, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cheng and Gallistel, 2014, Normand and Boesch, 2009, and Wilkie, 1989.

claim: The Grid Score measure compares the 2D spatial autocorrelation of the spike rate map to one that is rotated by 60 or 120 degrees versus one that is rotated 30, 90, or 150 degrees.
source: Using the 'Grid Score' measure developed by Solstad et al., 2008, even the first 1000 time steps produce a fairly accurate hexagonal grid of memory positions. The Grid Score measure compares the 2D spatial autocorrelation of the spike rate map to one that is rotated by 60 or 120 degrees (sixfold symmetry for a hexagonal grid) versus one that is rotated 30, 90, or 150 degrees (fourfold symmetry for a square grid).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Solstad et al., 2008.

claim: Cells habituate and rapidly reduce their firing rate by an order of magnitude when their preferred stimulus is presented without cessation.
source: However, in practice, cells habituate and rapidly reduce their firing rate by an order of magnitude when their preferred stimulus is presented without cessation (Abbott et al., 1997; Tsodyks and Markram, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abbott et al., 1997 and Tsodyks and Markram, 1997.

claim: The grid pattern tends to be less regular in a novel environment.
source: This lack of grid regularity for a novel environment has been reported (Barry et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barry et al., 2012.

claim: The grid array tends to align with a straight wall of the enclosure.
source: In real data, the grid array tends to align with a straight wall of the enclosure (Krupic et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krupic et al., 2015.

claim: Grid spacing tends to shrink with experience.
source: It has been reported that grid spacing tends to shrink with experience (Barry et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barry et al., 2012.

claim: Early work on place cells in mazes found strong sensitivity to head direction.
source: Indicating that head direction is an important part of place cell representations, early work on place cells in mazes found strong sensitivity to head direction, such that the place field is found in one direction of travel but not the other (McNaughton et al., 1983; Muller et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McNaughton et al., 1983 and Muller et al., 1994.

claim: Place cells can exhibit head direction sensitivity in open field recordings.
source: Place cells can exhibit a less extreme version of head direction sensitivity in open field recordings (Rubin et al., 2014), but the nature of the sensitivity is more complicated, depending on location of the animal relative to the place field center (Jercog et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rubin et al., 2014 and Jercog et al., 2019.

claim: Removal of head direction input to hippocampus affects place cell responses.
source: However, removal of head direction input to hippocampus affects place cell responses (Calton et al., 2003) and grid cell responses (Winter et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Calton et al., 2003.

claim: Removal of head direction input to hippocampus affects grid cell responses.
source: However, removal of head direction input to hippocampus affects place cell responses (Calton et al., 2003) and grid cell responses (Winter et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Winter et al., 2015.

claim: Grid cell modules exist with nearby grid cells having the same orientation, spacing, and distortion, but different spatial phases.
source: One of the key findings in the grid cell literature is the existence of anatomically arranged modules, with nearby grid cells having the same orientation, spacing, and distortion (i.e. the degree to which the grid is slightly elongated in a particular direction), but different spatial phases (Stensola et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stensola et al., 2012 and Yoon et al., 2013.

claim: The Kepler conjecture states that there are two ways in which equal-sized spheres can be arranged with the densest possible packing: face-centered cubic packing (FCP) and hexagonal close packing (HCP).
source: In this case, the arrangement of memories should follow the Kepler conjecture (Hales, 2005), which states that there are two ways in which equal-sized spheres can be arranged with the densest possible packing. Both solutions are hexagonal in nature, containing separate layers of spheres that are hexagonally arranged with the same orientation and spacing, but with different phases: face-centered cubic packing (FCP), entails three different hexagonal layers, whereas hexagonal close packing (HCP) entails two different hexagonal layers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hales, 2005.

claim: A coordination between grid cells of different grid spacings was recently observed.
source: This coordination between grid cells of different grid spacings was recently been observed (Waaga et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Waaga et al., 2022.

claim: Some mEC cells that initially appear to have a single place cell firing field are in truth grid cells when the box borders are removed.
source: In keeping with this result for simulated head direction cell h2, it has been reported that some mEC cells that initially appear to have a single place cell firing field are in truth grid cells when the box borders are removed – removing the borders reveals that there are additional grid fields outside the box (Savelli et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Savelli et al., 2008.

claim: Stensola et al., 2012 simultaneously recorded as many as 186 mEC grid cells in individual rats.
source: Stensola et al., 2012 simultaneously recorded as many as 186 mEC grid cells in individual rats, finding approximately four different grid modules for each animal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stensola et al., 2012.

claim: The ratio of grid spacing between modules was found to be approximately the square root of 2 when comparing modules that had grid spacing values that were close in value.
source: The ratio of grid spacing between modules was found to be approximately the square root of 2 when comparing modules that had grid spacing values that were close in value.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from Stensola et al., 2012 data.

claim: A deformation of the enclosure caused some of the grid modules but not others to undergo a deformation of the grid pattern.
source: This might explain why a deformation of the enclosure (moving one of the walls to form a rectangle rather than a square) caused some of the grid modules but not others to undergo a deformation of the grid pattern in response to the deformation of the enclosure wall (see also Barry et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barry et al., 2007.

claim: Grid field patterns are often seen immediately upon entry into a novel environment.
source: However, grid field patterns are often seen immediately upon entry into a novel environment, although the pattern may be somewhat less regular for a novel environment (Barry et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barry et al., 2012.

claim: Place cells take time to stabilize their positions.
source: This slow stabilization of place fields is a known property (Bostock et al., 1991; Frank et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bostock et al., 1991 and Frank et al., 2004.

claim: Encounters with boundaries can serve to stabilize grid fields.
source: Considering that place fields are the cause of individual grid fields for the model, this may relate to the finding that encounters with boundaries can serve to stabilize grid fields (Hardcastle et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hardcastle et al., 2015.

claim: Pattern separation causes memories to push against each other during consolidation.
source: More specifically, memories initially formed inside the box in positions adjacent to the borders push against each other during consolidation owing to pattern separation (Chanales et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chanales et al., 2017.

claim: The faces of famous individuals are more easily recognized when drawn with impossibly exaggerated facial features.
source: By analogy, the faces of famous individuals are more easily recognized when drawn with impossibly exaggerated facial features (Mauro and Kubovy, 1992)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mauro and Kubovy, 1992.

claim: Grid cells can exist even during sleep.
source: Another class of grid cell models propose that the grid emerges from intrinsic attractor dynamics within entorhinal cortex (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Couey et al., 2013; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Guanella et al., 2007; McNaughton et al., 2006), explaining why the grid can exist even during sleep (Gardner et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2019.

claim: Human entorhinal cortex exhibits grid-like responses to video morph trajectories in a two-dimensional bird neck-length versus bird leg-length space.
source: For instance, human entorhinal cortex exhibits grid-like responses to video morph trajectories in a two-dimensional bird neck-length versus bird leg-length space (Constantinescu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Constantinescu et al., 2016.

claim: Well-learned non-spatial two-dimensional spaces such as pine/banana odors produce grid-like responses.
source: This might explain why well-learned non-spatial two-dimensional spaces such as cartoon bird neck/leg length (Constantinescu et al., 2016) and pine/banana odors (Bao et al., 2019) produce grid-like responses in areas other than the MTL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bao et al., 2019.

claim: Visual search in the two dimensions of the visual field can produce grid-like responses in humans.
source: It might also explain why visual search in the two dimensions of the visual field can produce grid-like responses in humans (Julian et al., 2018) and primates (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Julian et al., 2018.

claim: Visual search in the two dimensions of the visual field can produce grid-like responses in primates.
source: It might also explain why visual search in the two dimensions of the visual field can produce grid-like responses in humans (Julian et al., 2018) and primates (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Killian et al., 2012.

claim: Inactivation of the hippocampus eliminates grid responses.
source: Subsequent work called into question these models (although see Lian and Burkitt, 2022), based on the finding that inactivation of the hippocampus eliminates grid responses (Bonnevie et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bonnevie et al., 2013.

claim: Place cells exist before grid cells during development.
source: and the finding that place cells exist before grid cells during development (Bjerknes et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bjerknes et al., 2014.

claim: Non-spatial hippocampal memory encoding has been found in rodents.
source: Other literatures with other species find non-spatial representations in MTL (Gulli et al., 2020; Quiroga et al., 2005; Wixted et al., 2014) and non-spatial hippocampal memory encoding has been found in rodents (Liu et al., 2012; McEchron and Disterhoft, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012 and McEchron and Disterhoft, 1999.

claim: Non-spatial representations in MTL have been found in other species.
source: Other literatures with other species find non-spatial representations in MTL (Gulli et al., 2020; Quiroga et al., 2005; Wixted et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gulli et al., 2020, Quiroga et al., 2005, and Wixted et al., 2014.

claim: Hippocampus can explicitly represent the passage of time.
source: However, there is evidence that hippocampus can explicitly represent the passage of time (Eichenbaum, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eichenbaum, 2014.

claim: Manipulations of grid spacing are associated with an increase in the size of place fields.
source: This recurrence might explain the finding that manipulations of grid spacing are associated with an increase in the size of place fields (Mallory et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mallory et al., 2018.

claim: Multifield grid cells for freely flying bats have a systematic minimum distance between firing fields, but their arrangement is globally irregular.
source: This may explain why the multifield grid cells for freely flying bats have a systematic minimum distance between firing fields, but their arrangement is globally irregular (Ginosar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ginosar et al., 2021.

claim: Mathematicians studying the 'sphere packing problem' recently concluded that densest packing in four dimensions is irregular.
source: Furthermore, in the case of four dimensions, mathematicians studying the 'sphere packing problem' recently concluded that densest packing is irregular (Campos et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Campos et al., 2023.

claim: Place cells support memories of the locations where non-spatial attributes can be found, which are arranged in a hexagonal lattice owing to memory encoding and consolidation processes.
source: Place cells support memories of the locations where non-spatial attributes can be found (e.g. positions with a particular sound), which are arranged in a hexagonal lattice owing to memory encoding and consolidation processes (pattern separation) as applied to situations in which the non-spatial attributes are found at all locations of a two-dimensional surface.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the model.

claim: The model predicts that place cells lie on a torus defined by circular border cells.
source: More specifically, the model predicts that place cells lie on a torus defined by circular border cells and because place cells are the cause the grid fields, the population code of grid cells also lies on a torus.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the model based on its architecture.

claim: The model is one of the first computational models to explain the toroidal nature of grid cells.
source: This is one of the first computational models to explain the toroidal nature of grid cells (but see Guanella et al., 2007; McNaughton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model with citations to prior models.

claim: Border cells are not always uniform in their responsiveness along a particular border.
source: Border cells are not always uniform in their responsiveness along a particular border (Solstad et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Solstad et al., 2008.

claim: The model predicts the existence of cells that fire between the borders, but not at the border, although such cells are relatively rare.
source: In addition, the model predicts the existence of cells that fire between the borders, but not at the border, although such cells are relatively rare (Solstad et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a prediction made by the model with citation to empirical data.

claim: The model has the potential to explain context effects in memory.
source: This model has the potential to explain context effects in memory (Godden and Baddeley, 1975; Gulli et al., 2020; Howard et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's potential with citations to context effects literature.

claim: The model assumes that cells avoid firing constantly at their maximum possible rate during the entire recording session.
source: Because the non-spatial attribute is common to all positions (e.g. the electronic noise occurs everywhere), and because various mechanisms ensure that cells avoid firing constantly at their maximum possible rate during the entire recording session, grid cells fire preferentially in the locations of each memory.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a model assumption.

claim: The model assumes divisive normalization and inhibitory interneurons allow cells to adjust their firing threshold.
source: Rather than firing at a constant high rate regardless of location, the cell adopts an adjusted firing threshold owing to inhibitory interneurons and divisive normalization (Bhatia et al., 2019; Carandini and Heeger, 2011; Olsen et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhatia et al., 2019, Carandini and Heeger, 2011, and Olsen et al., 2010.

claim: The proposed consolidation process might arise from several cycles of alternating bottom-up memory activation and top-down memory recall as coordinated by theta oscillations.
source: In real systems, the proposed consolidation process might arise from several cycles of alternating bottom-up memory activation and top-down memory recall as coordinated by theta oscillations (see Ólafsdóttir et al., 2016 for evidence that something similar might occur during offline consolidation).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ólafsdóttir et al., 2016.

claim: The model predicts that in the absence of memory retrieval from hippocampal place cells, each mEC grid cell should revert to its underlying bottom-up receptive field.
source: A key prediction of this account is that in the absence of memory retrieval from hippocampal place cells, each mEC grid cell should revert to its underlying bottom-up receptive field.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model prediction.

claim: In the absence of hippocampal feedback, a head direction conjunctive grid cell should become a head direction cell at all positions rather than just at grid field positions.
source: For instance, in the absence of top-down memory retrieval feedback, a head direction conjunctive grid cell should become a head direction cell at all positions rather than just at grid field positions. Such a finding was reported by Bonnevie et al., 2013.
evidence: This is a prediction that is supported by citation to Bonnevie et al., 2013.

claim: The model predicts that place cell fields should be arrayed in a hexagonal grid for situations that produce grid cell firing.
source: This model predicts that place cell fields should be arrayed in a hexagonal grid for situations that produce grid cell firing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model prediction.

claim: The model predicts a one-to-one correspondence between each grid field of a particular grid cell and a corresponding place field.
source: Once a set of place cells is identified in this manner, the place field centers of the set should be arrayed in the same manner as the grid cell used to identify the set. In other words, there should be a one-to-one correspondence between each grid field of a particular grid cell and a corresponding place field.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model prediction.

claim: The model predicts that hexagonally arranged grid cells should be the exception rather than the rule when considering more naturalistic environments.
source: According to this model, hexagonally arranged grid cells should be the exception rather than the rule when considering more naturalistic environments.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model prediction.

claim: Even in a situation where there are regular hexagonal grid cells, there are often irregular non-grid cells that have a reliable multi-location firing field.
source: This may explain the finding that even in a situation where there are regular hexagonal grid cells, there are often irregular non-grid cells that have a reliable multi-location firing field, but the arrangement of the firing fields is irregular (Diehl et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Diehl et al., 2017.

claim: The model predicts that grid-like responses do not require spatial navigation for their existence.
source: This memory model predicts that grid-like responses do not require spatial navigation for their existence.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model prediction.

claim: The model predicts that grid-like responses might occur in any situation involving a highly familiar two-dimensional space in which nothing of interest varies aside from the two dimensions.
source: Instead, grid-like responses might occur in any situation involving a highly familiar two-dimensional space in which nothing of interest varies aside from the two dimensions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a model prediction.

claim: The model assumes that LEC is the source of non-spatial what information for memory encoding.
source: One possible answer to the apparent lack of non-spatial cells in MTL is to highlight the role of the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) as the source of non-spatial what information for memory encoding (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011.

claim: mEC appears to only provide where information.
source: LEC can be contrasted with mEC, which appears to only provide where information (Boccara et al., 2010; Diehl et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boccara et al., 2010 and Diehl et al., 2017.

claim: The model simulations used three non-orthogonal E/F/G circular dimensions.
source: To achieve Euclidean representations, the reported simulations used three non-orthogonal E/F/G circular dimensions (Figure 3C), which define a space that is a hexagonally connected three-dimensional torus.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model implementation.

claim: With three non-orthogonal dimensions, the similarity between memories is approximately Euclidean.
source: With three non-orthogonal dimensions, the similarity between memories is approximately Euclidean (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing the relationship.

claim: With two orthogonal dimensions, the similarity between memories follows a city-block metric.
source: In contrast, with two orthogonal dimensions, the similarity between memories follows a city-block metric.

claim: The model assumes that when a memory is formed, a hippocampal place cell is recruited and the weights connecting the place cell to the entorhinal inputs are set equal to the current input values.

evidence: This is a direct statement about the model mechanism with citation.

claim: The model assumes that the weights between the entorhinal inputs and the place cells are bidirectional.

evidence: This is a direct statement about the model architecture visible in Figure 2.

claim: The model assumes that memory consolidation produces unbiased memory representations that tile the environment.
source: The representations of memories are altered by an online consolidation process that produces unbiased memory representations that tile the environment (i.e. a cognitive map).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's consolidation process.

claim: The model assumes that consolidation pushes memories to become maximally dissimilar through pattern separation.
source: After initial memory retrieval, the retrieved inputs are used to activate the competing memories and this strength of activation of competitors is compared to a consolidation threshold, θc (yellow dashed circle, centered on retrieved memory), which is smaller than the activation threshold, such that consolidation pushes memories to become maximally dissimilar (pattern separation).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's consolidation mechanism.

claim: The model assumes that competing memories that are more active than the consolidation threshold push the weights of the retrieved memory away from the competing memory.
source: Competing memories that are more active than the consolidation threshold (red dot) push the weights of the retrieved memory away from the competing memory (red arrow).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's consolidation mechanism.

claim: The model assumes that competing memories that are less active than the consolidation threshold pull the weights of the retrieved memory towards the competing memory.
source: Competing memories that are less active than the consolidation threshold (green dot) pull the weights of the retrieved memory towards the competing memory (green arrow).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's consolidation mechanism.

claim: For memories arranged in two real-world dimensions, consolidation typically results in activation of three surrounding memories and makes the triangle formed by these memories an equilateral triangle.
source: For memories arranged in two real-world dimensions, this typically results in activation of three surrounding memories and consolidation makes the triangle formed by these memories an equilateral triangle (gray arrow).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's consolidation outcome.
